name: pocketpy
workload: Elapsed time of benchmarks/primes.py at commit 9481d653 (Atkin sieve of primes up to 5,000,000, trie build over the primes as strings, prefix search for 32338) run by pkpy 1.2.7 and by CPython; Lua 5.3.3 and a C++ gnu++11 port of the same program are listed beside them.
claimed_speedup: pkpy 1.2.7 2.385s vs CPython 3.8.10 2.871s (about 1.2x faster, derived from page data); README text: 'Currently, pkpy is as fast as cpython 3.9.' For context the same table has Lua 5.3.3 at 1.576s (faster than pkpy) and C++ at 0.104s.
stars_or_usage: 2.1k stars; used by TIC-80, Godot extension, Flutter plugin (README 'Used By')
tradeoffs: Portable Python 3.x subset interpreter in C11 with no dependencies beyond libc (single header + source amalgamation), aimed at game scripting as a Lua alternative; not full CPython compatible and has no JIT. README says NDEBUG must be defined for release builds or performance is poor.
caveats: Numbers are for pkpy 1.2.7, an earlier C++ implementation; the repo has since been rewritten as the 2.x C11 interpreter, and docs/performance.md (raw.githubusercontent.com/pocketpy/pocketpy/HEAD/docs/performance.md) now labels the 1.2.7 table 'historical ... not a benchmark of the current 2.x C11 interpreter' and says results from one script do not predict other programs. Single workload, single run per row (repeat count and median not stated), build flags and compiler for pkpy not stated, CPython 3.8.10 is old (3.11+ is substantially faster), and Lua is faster than pkpy on the same program. The README claim 'as fast as cpython 3.9' is generalised beyond the one table (which itself lists CPython 3.8.10). Benchmark sources are public (benchmarks/primes.py, primes.cpp, primes.lua), so it can be rerun, but the tier stays C because flags are missing and the run is first-party.

name: QuickJS
workload: Octane-style JavaScript scores (higher is better) from the javascript-zoo-data CI harness: QuickJS d73189dd (2026-05-21) from bench/amd64/quickjs.json and quickjs_gcc.json, Duktape from bench/amd64/duktape.json (gcc 16.1.0) and duktape_clang.json (clang 23.0.0); 14 tests completed by both engines (Richards, DeltaBlue, Crypto, RayTrace, EarleyBoyer, RegExp, Splay, SplayLatency, NavierStokes, PdfJS, Box2D, CodeLoad, Gameboy, zlib). Duktape could not complete Typescript, Mandreel or MandreelLatency.
claimed_speedup: Medians of the listed score arrays (derived from page data), QuickJS built with clang 23.0.0 vs Duktape built with clang 23.0.0: Richards 746 vs 385, DeltaBlue 784 vs 438, EarleyBoyer 2130 vs 894, Splay 3394 vs 1358, Box2D 3219 vs 1952, PdfJS 3816 vs 519 (7.3x), Crypto 854 vs 854 (tie); geometric mean ratio 1.97x over the 14 common tests (derived), QuickJS ahead on 13 of 14. Both built with gcc 16.1.0 (quickjs_gcc.json vs duktape.json): geometric mean 1.60x, ahead on 11 of 14, behind on Crypto (417 vs 1068), NavierStokes (1150 vs 1372) and zlib (666 vs 751).
compiler_and_flags: QuickJS: clang 23.0.0 at -O3, no LTO (javascript-zoo engines/quickjs/Dockerfile sets OPT=-O3); also gcc 16.1.0 build. Duktape: same two compilers, Makefile patched from -Os to -O3 (engines/duktape/Dockerfile). Compiler versions come from the result files; flags from the public Dockerfiles.
tradeoffs: Interpreter only, no JIT; full recent ECMAScript (ESnext per javascript-zoo) with reference counting plus cycle collector; larger than Duktape (Bellard's page: 620K vs 331K executable); built binary 1.18 MB in the zoo build.
caveats: Independent aggregator (ivankra/javascript-zoo), not peer reviewed; the CPU model of the machine that produced the result files is not recorded in the JSON (amd64 CI runner), so the tier stays B. Comparison engine is an old Duktape revision (2024-01-29). Result depends strongly on compiler: the zoo's own Dockerfile comment says clang builds of QuickJS are significantly faster than gcc builds, and with gcc QuickJS loses on Crypto, NavierStokes and zlib. The result files hold per-run score arrays, so the per-test figures and ratios above are my medians and geometric means (derived). Only part of the dataset was opened; zoo.js.org (the rendered tables) was unreachable here. Older first-party evidence, opened only through the Chinese mirror https://raw.githubusercontent.com/quickjs-zh/QuickJS/HEAD/bench.md because bellard.org was unreachable (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND): bench-v8 v7 totals QuickJS 942 vs Duktape 2.3.0 408 (about 2.3x), gcc 4.9.2 -O2, 3.2 GHz Core i5 4570, QuickJS 2019-07-09; the bench-v8 sources ship in the release archive, not the GitHub tree.

name: SWIG
baseline: SWIG's own default Python proxy-class wrappers (same tool, default code generation mode)
workload: Per-call overhead, in microseconds, of calling three member functions of a trivial C++ class Go from Python through SWIG-generated wrappers: callme0() with no arguments, callme4() with four ints, callme8() with eight doubles; default proxy classes vs the -fastproxy option vs the -builtin option.
claimed_speedup: Default 0.15 / 0.26 / 0.32 us; -fastproxy 0.09 / 0.16 / 0.20 us (about 1.6-1.7x lower, derived from page data); -builtin 0.07 / 0.14 / 0.17 us (about 1.9-2.1x lower, derived from page data). Manual text: '-builtin ... significant performance improvement in the wrapped code'.
tradeoffs: -fastproxy makes generated proxy classes less user-friendly (docstrings, annotations and default arguments are not visible) and is ignored for methods with %pythonprepend-style extra code; -builtin replaces proxy classes with built-in types and does not use the Python limited API. Both are Python-only options; the per-call numbers are for Python, other target languages have no comparable table.
caveats: The baseline is SWIG's own default mode, not another binding tool: the manual makes no numeric comparison against SIP, pybind11, Boost.Python or Cython, and a WebSearch for third-party SWIG call-overhead numbers found none. No hardware, compiler, Python version or repeat count is stated, so this is a first-party, partial-methodology result (tier C). Another table in the same manual shows the -threads option slowing the profiletest.i run (single threaded 9.6 s vs fully multithreaded 15.5 s). LICENSE: SWIG itself is GPL-3.0-or-later with portions under LICENSE-UNIVERSITIES; Lib and Examples are under a permissive grant; the lead's tag says generated output is not licensed (not independently verified).

name: TensorFlow
workload: Training throughput of ResNet-50 v1.5 (images/sec, automatic mixed precision) and BERT-base pretraining (sentences/sec, AMP) on 1 to 32 Tesla V100-SXM2-16GB GPUs (4 nodes x 8) using NVIDIA DeepLearningExamples scripts; the TensorFlow side is NGC TensorFlow 1.15.2 (nvcr.io/nvidia/tensorflow:20.03-tf1-py3) with XLA, and stock TensorFlow 2.3.0 with tensorflow/models scripts.
claimed_speedup: ResNet-50 v1.5 AMP, NGC TensorFlow 1.x with XLA (bsz=224) vs NGC PyTorch: 1198.55 vs 802.9 img/s on 1 GPU, 8588.45 vs 6154.66 on 8 GPUs, 29171.69 vs 22551.16 on 32 GPUs (about 1.49x, 1.40x, 1.29x, derived from page data). BERT-base AMP bsz=max, same pair: 468.10 vs 462.35, 3559.8 vs 3287.12 and 11650.0 vs 10349.12 sentences/s on 1, 8 and 32 GPUs (about 1.01x, 1.08x, 1.13x, derived). Stock TensorFlow 2.3.0 AMP ResNet-50: 1075.27 img/s (1 GPU) and 6898.00 (8 GPUs), above NGC PyTorch there, but 19314.31 on 32 GPUs, below 22551.16.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (prebuilt NVIDIA NGC containers 20.03 for TensorFlow 1.15.2 and PyTorch 1.5.0a0; TensorFlow 2.3.0 and PyTorch 1.6.0 installed separately); CUDA 10.2, driver 440.33.01; XLA and AMP enabled per run as listed in the report.
hardware: 4 nodes, each 8x Tesla V100-SXM2-16GB, Intel Xeon Gold 5118 @ 2.30GHz, 384 GB RAM, InfiniBand 100 Gb/s EDR, Ubuntu 16.04.4
tradeoffs: XLA and AMP need extra configuration, and the TensorFlow 1.x XLA run used a smaller per-GPU batch (224) than PyTorch (256) to avoid out-of-memory; TensorFlow 1.x is end-of-life, TensorFlow 2.x is the maintained line.
caveats: Mixed evidence, not a clean win. The suite is run by OneFlow (a competing framework) in October 2020 and the numbers are six years old. The wins come from NVIDIA's NGC build of TensorFlow 1.15.2 with XLA plus AMP, not the stock tensorflow/tensorflow v2.3.0 tree, and mostly against NVIDIA's NGC PyTorch examples. In FP32 PyTorch is faster: ResNet-50 bsz=128 on 32 GPUs, NGC TensorFlow 1.x 9514.64 vs NGC PyTorch 10917.09 img/s and TensorFlow 2.x 9418.44 vs PyTorch 1.6.0 10021.29 (README and report tables); stock TensorFlow 2.3.0 BERT is also slower than NGC PyTorch (README: FP32 2244.38 vs 3039.3 sentences/s at bsz=max). The stock PyTorch examples were not run with AMP in the report. XLA vs no-XLA gains inside TensorFlow (e.g. BERT AMP 11650.0 w/XLA at bsz=96 vs 5189.07 without XLA at bsz=64) are TensorFlow-vs-TensorFlow and are not counted as a win over PyTorch. The tier is B, not A, because compiler and build flags of the containers are not stated and the batch sizes differ between the compared rows. Google's own XLA blog post was not opened.
